blocks.text: to the Paphian birds, that is, to doves. Indeed, like the karia of the Arabs, the scolopax too, or woodcock (rusticula), is a harbinger of rain. Gesner in his Birds, p. 504: Some make the call of the lesser woodcock (the French call it beccassine), when heard, a prognostic of rain. He adds that the sound of its call is like that of a knife drawn across a saw. This seems to be what the Arabs mean when they attribute to the karia ترجيع [tarjīʿ], that is, a reciprocating call. So far, then, everything is quite similar. The colour, however, is different: in the karia it is green, at least on the back, while in the woodcock it is so mottled that it is very far from green. Moreover, although both birds are edible, David does not seem to have held the קורא kore in great esteem; and the Arabs celebrate the karia for no other reason than that it is among the prognostics of rain. Our woodcock, by contrast, is most renowned among the delicacies of the table, and yields little to the partridge. Hence Martial, book 13, Epigram 76, under the heading Rusticula: [II, 636] Whether I am a woodcock or a partridge, what does it matter, if the flavour is the same? The partridge is dearer; that is why it tastes better.

Finally, no one has written of the woodcock what Jeremiah wrote of the קורא kore: the kore gathered (or sat on eggs) and did not bring forth. I conclude, therefore, that the kore is a bird peculiar to those regions, distinct from the woodcock, yet not differing from it greatly ^{(2)}. We must now state how the ancient and modern interpreters explain this word.

Kore קרא is rendered by the Greeks νυκτικόραξ [nyktikorax], nycticorax, 1 Sam. XXVI, 20., but they were doubtless misled by a faulty reading. They had evidently read קדא for קרא, Daleth for Resh, letters that are very similar to each other. The word קדא ceased to be in use among the Hebrews; but from it the Chaldeans formed קדיא, and the Syrians ܥܕܝܢ, with Koph and Ayin interchanged, as when they say ܥܛܪ, vapour, for קטר, and ܥܪܝܐ, cold, for [II, 637] קריא. That this conjecture is correct is evident from the fact that elsewhere in the Greek version νυκτικόραξ [nyktikorax] corresponds to the Hebrew כוס, for which the Chaldee Onkelos has קריא, Levit. XI, 17., and the Syriac translator ܒܣܢ, Psal. CII, 7. Therefore כוס and קרא, whence קריא and ܒܣܢ, are synonyms. So if כוס is the νυκτικόραξ [nyktikorax], as the Greeks render it, so too is קרא. There is a similar error in the Talmudic tractate Niddah, fol. 23a, where instead of קדיא with Daleth, קריא with Resh is written eight times, as if it were the bird kore, whereas it is a night bird. For joined to it is קפופא kiphupha, that is, the owl. And they are said to be birds דעיניהן הולכות לפניהן כשלאדם, whose eyes are not at the side, as in other birds, but in front, as in humans. And in the Gloss both are described as עוף צועק בלילה ופניו דומות לחתול ועיניו לפניו, a bird that cries at night, with a face like a cat's and eyes in front. Again in Berakhot, ch. 9, fol. 57b: כל מינין עופית יפין לחלום חוץ מן קריא וקפופא וקורפראי, All species of birds are auspicious in dreams, except the nycticorax, the owl and the bat. In these words too, I say, קריא is written with Resh, which must be changed to Daleth. So finally in the Chaldee [col. 84] paraphrase of Es. XXXIV, 15., for וקורידהון ינצפון בטולה read וקודידהון, And their nycticoraces shall howl in its shade. For there too Resh stands for Daleth. This is why the Latin translator of the Chaldee rendered it thus: And the partridges shall chatter, etc. This is utterly absurd. For the passage concerns the devastation of Edom, to which it is not fitting that partridges should chatter in it, but that nycticoraces and eagle-owls should howl in a horrifying manner.
